findings.title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes
findings.body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write builds its 10-second timeout context as a child of the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Request contexts in the apiserver are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and in these methods the goroutine is started right before `return`, i.e. typically before the response is fully flushed. This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

findings.title: Delete records the object name where the metric kind label is expected
findings.body: On the success path of DualWriterMode3.Delete, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object `name` in the position of the `kind` label (compare with the error path on line 103 which correctly passes `options.Kind`). Every successful delete will emit a metric labeled with the deleted object's name instead of the resource kind, polluting metric label cardinality (one label value per object name) and making per-kind delete latency dashboards wrong.

findings.title: Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy-storage metric failures
findings.body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the async legacy result with recordStorageDuration
findings.body: In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, as done in Create/Delete/Update. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors will be attributed to the unified storage metric, corrupting both series.

findings.title: Delete injects d.Log into the context instead of the enriched per-request logger
findings.body: In Delete, the enriched logger `log` (built with name, kind and method values) is created on line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, injecting the base logger instead of `log`. Every other method injects the enriched `log`. The consequence is that any log lines emitted from the request context in Delete (and the error log on line 102) are missing the name/kind/method fields that all other mode 3 methods provide, producing inconsistent structured logs.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's (possibly stale) object, dropping the previous updateWrapper protection
findings.body: The previous mode 3 Update wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` so the legacy store wrote the exact object produced by the unified-store update. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

findings.title: Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
findings.body: In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous legacy writes, making them racy and non-verifying
findings.body: The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests assert legacy API state immediately after async k8s writes, which is inherently flaky
findings.body: The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous with no synchronization, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the create/update when these assertions run, causing intermittent failures (or, worse, passing while the write is silently dropped). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

findings.title: Delete no longer falls back to legacy storage when the unified store returns NotFound
findings.body: The replaced implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted the object from legacy storage. The new Delete returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so if an object exists only in legacy storage (e.g. incompletely migrated), a mode 3 delete returns NotFound to the client and the orphaned legacy row is never removed. If mode 3 is meant to be a 'safe measure' that keeps legacy in sync, the NotFound-tolerant fallback for the legacy delete should be preserved; otherwise this behavior change should be documented as intentional.
